rationale: The inverse-image bracket opened before F_{ni} is closed by a parenthesis in the authority, leaving the formula unbalanced.  Closing the bracket before the outer measure parenthesis restores the intended set expression.

The displayed composition identity has one unmatched closing parenthesis after the argument of the image measure.  Removing it restores balanced application syntax and agrees with the preceding and following lines.
The proposition requires the sum of positive-part integrals; without the integral sign the expression is not a scalar and conflicts with the proof in 234H(c)(iii).
The proposition requires the sum of negative-part integrals; without the integral sign the expression is not a scalar and conflicts with the proof in 234H(c)(iii).
Only E and F are introduced in this proof.  Completeness of each mu_i yields E in Sigma_i from E subseteq F and mu_i F=0; no indexed E_i exists.

The proposition and the two preceding occurrences concern extended-real integrals on [-infinity,infinity].  Repeating positive infinity as both endpoints collapses the interval and contradicts the equivalence being proved.

The essential-supremum equivalence measures H minus the union of H' and X minus G.  The authority has an unmatched extra opening parenthesis and fails to close the measure application; the corrected grouping is balanced and yields the next equivalence.
The theorem assumes that nu is an indefinite-integral measure over mu.  Referring to nu as its own base measure contradicts the theorem statement and the cited consequences, all of which use mu.
The equality expands nu F minus mu F term by term.  Without grouping, only the nu terms are summed and a single free n remains in the mu term; parentheses make both terms part of every summand.
The finite choice is made from the sum of the differences defining lambda G_n.  Without parentheses only nu F_n is summed and the final mu F_n has a free index.
The equality uses finite additivity for nu F minus mu F.  Both terms must be grouped inside the sum; otherwise the displayed equality leaves the last mu term unsummed.
The exercise defines Sigma as a sigma-algebra on X and then defines mu on X.  Tau is the sigma-algebra on Y, so E belongs to Sigma; using Tau is a type error.
